doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: Composing from everyday rhythms
summary: White finds rhythm in trains, fans and windshield wipers and builds melody from it, thinking of phrases before chords.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: especially to things that have rhythm. I realized in the old days the train was a very important part of, you know early blues and jazz, the rhythm of the train and the symbolism of the train. It represented progress, it represented movement, it represented freedom, it represented going north and all of those things. But at the same time it gave great rhythms that you could, you know, take off on on songs. So now I try to hear rhythm through things. And It’s simple things now that catch my attention. It might be an old rickety fan as it turns around and maybe a certain rhythm in that. I remember going to the cleaners, the dry cleaners a couple of months ago and hearing that and I recorded it. And I came home and wrote a song based on that rhythm. But nowadays things like the windshield wiper gives a lot of good rhythm. It might be a clothes dryer, a washing machine, something like that. So you, you know, and I use that not only in the avant garde kind of stuff but in traditional music too.
Say how do you – if you compose a melody with that particular rhythm as an inspiration do you then move on to, “Well I need some chord structure here?” Or do you try not to think that way?
